title: Letter 39 — The Chastening Hand of God
attribution_note: Letter 39 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

sections.heading: War and plague upon the fatherland

pairs.en: We see now, Christians, the chastening hand of God upon us; we see how greatly our fatherland sighs and groans under the bloody war with the Turk: many fall and are wounded by the weapon of the foreigner; mothers and fathers weep for their sons, wives for their husbands, brethren for a brother fallen or wounded; the treasury is emptied and grows poor, men grow fewer, in a word, the whole fatherland endures adversity and is in confusion. But to this calamity another, no less grievous, has been added: the pestilence has grown strong, and here and there one hears of distress. All this we see, and we sigh, and we weep, and we bear the chastisement.

But we must confess from the heart that in this there is our fault and our unrighteousness. We must, bowing our heads, acknowledge and confess before God: *“To Thee, O Lord, belongeth righteousness, but unto us confusion of faces”* [Daniel 9:7]. *“Thou art righteous, O Lord, and all Thy judgments are just;* *Thou art righteous, O Lord, and there is no unrighteousness in Thee”* [Tobit 3:2].

If we look upon our works, we shall see our great shame and our great unrighteousness before God. To break an oath given before God and His holy Gospel is counted among us as a jest. The places of judgment, where the judgment of God is administered, have been made a marketplace and a traffic. Truth and justice have been cast down from their throne, and in their place mammon sits and lifts up its voice. Come not to the court without money: thou shalt find nothing. For a landlord to take five or six roubles a year from a single peasant in the Ukraine, where bread is cheap and money dear, is counted as nothing. It is counted a small thing that three days in the week a man must labour for his landlord, not reckoning other works, and from them the poll-tax also is taken.
Great is the unrighteousness, and great the self-love!

Where shall those burdened with such dues and labours find what they need for themselves? Where — what is needful for the wife, the children, and the rest of the household? Whence bread, food, clothing, shoes, and a dwelling? And when shall they take rest, for the flesh is weak? Thus some groan under landlords, others under judges unjust and corrupted by bribes, and their groanings enter into the ears of God. Like unrighteousness is found in the merchant estate, among the peasantry, and in every rank. It is counted a small thing, or as nothing, to deceive, to beguile, to seize another's goods, to defile a neighbour's bed, to work malice and take revenge, to wound a neighbour with a word and blacken him by slander, or to destroy him.
Behold our works! Behold our Christianity!

sections.heading: God calls, and we do not hearken

pairs.en: God calls us to repentance — we do not hearken to Him.
God sent His Son to us to save us — we do not hearken to Him.
He suffered for our sins — we give no heed to this, and we repeat our sins.
God forbade us to wrong one another, forbade us to steal, to bear false witness, forbade us to covet another's goods — we do not hearken to Him.
God commanded us to love one another, to do good one to another — we do not hearken to Him.
He commanded the judges to keep the truth — they do not hearken to Him.
He commanded all to depart from evil and to do good (cf. Psalm 33:15) — we give no heed to this.
He feeds us, clothes us, and supplies us with the other goods of this world — we do not hearken to Him, and we render no thanksgiving to our Benefactor.

God looks upon this our disobedience, looks, and sees, and writes it in His book. What remains, then, but that the righteousness of God should enter into its work? Men do not feel the mercy of God when He shows them mercy — God is constrained to make His righteousness known. We would not know the mercy of God toward us and so be thankful to Him; behold, now we have known the working of the righteousness of God. And they who are not moved even by this chastisement — a sign that they have hearts hardened — shall know upon themselves the eternal judgment of the righteousness of God.

Therefore let us turn with all the heart; *“O come, let us weep before the Lord that made us”* [Psalm 94:6]. Let us all with one accord lift up the voice of our heart: *“Let Thy tender mercies speedily prevent us, O Lord”* [Psalm 78:8], and the rest. Thus praying and repenting of our sins, let us cease from our sins and hate them as our enemies, who before God, as fierce and stinking accusers, slander us and stir up His righteous wrath against us and bring manifold chastisements upon us. Let us cease to provoke the righteous God and to grieve His goodness, that what we see upon our brethren may not draw near to us also. For we are in nothing better than they. Let us bring forth *“fruits worthy of repentance”* [Matthew 3:8].
Judges! Keep the truth as the apple of the eye.
Priests! Forget not your calling, who ye are and whereunto ye are chosen.
Masters! Spare your poor peasants.
Ye clerks! Write, and do not overthrow the truth, and be content with the dues appointed you by the Monarchess, and stretch not forth your hands to another's goods.
Merchants! Carry on your trade without wrong, without lying, without unrighteousness.
All other men, do not unto your neighbours that which ye would not have done unto yourselves.
Ye extortioners! Leave off extortion.
Ye fornicators! Leave off fornication, and love purity.
Ye drunkards! Love sobriety.
Ye thieves and robbers! Cease to wrong your neighbours.
Ye slanderers and mockers! Amend your tongue.
Ye that are at enmity! Be reconciled, and love the Christian peace.

So God, seeing our amendment, will incline to mercy toward us, and, hearing the groaning of our hearts, will have mercy upon us according to His great mercy. But if there be no amendment, then must every man look for not only temporal but also eternal punishment — which suffer not, O God, according to Thy mercy. Amen.
